title: Rachel's longing (Genesis 30:1–24)
hook: years of waiting, then Joseph; the family grows through rivalry and prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday: Leah's sons, named seen, heard and joined, and then Judah: this time, praise.

Rachel is the loved one. Jacob worked fourteen years for her. She watches her sister have one son, then two, three, four. She has none. The Torah doesn't make her gracious about it: she envied her sister. She goes to Jacob and says, in the old JPS translation: "Give me children, or else I die." It's one of the rawest sentences in Genesis. Anyone who has waited for a child, or for anything everyone around them seems to get easily, knows that voice. Jacob, who loves her, snaps: "Am I in God's stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?" Two people who love each other, both in pain, saying the wrong thing.
screen: `THE LOVED ONE, WITH NO CHILD.` → `GIVE ME CHILDREN, OR ELSE I DIE.` → `AM I IN GOD'S STEAD?`

segments.voice: What follows is messy, and the Torah tells it straight. Rachel gives Jacob her servant Bilhah, and names Bilhah's sons herself. One she calls Naphtali, from wrestling: I have wrestled mightily with my sister, and I have prevailed. Leah answers with her own servant, and more sons. The sisters even bargain over mandrakes, a plant people believed helped with fertility. Rivalry, out in the open. Then, at last: "And God remembered Rachel, and God hearkened to her, and opened her womb." She has a son and names him Joseph, Yosef, may He add: may God add another son to me. Even her joy has longing in it. But the rabbis saw more in Rachel than rivalry. The Talmud tells that before the wedding, Jacob and Rachel had agreed on secret signs, so Laban couldn't switch the bride. When Rachel saw Leah led to the tent, she gave Leah the signs, so Leah wouldn't be shamed. She gave away her own wedding night to protect her sister. A midrash tells that centuries later, when Jerusalem fell and the patriarchs pleaded with God for their children, God was silent, until Rachel spoke: I overcame my jealousy of my sister. God answered her. The prophet Jeremiah hears Rachel weeping for her children, refusing to be comforted, and God telling her to hold back her tears, for there is hope. Rachel wanted honestly, fought honestly, gave generously, and prayed. The tradition doesn't ask her to pretend. Her longing is part of why she's heard.
screen: `NAPHTALI — I HAVE WRESTLED.` · `GOD REMEMBERED RACHEL.` · `YOSEF — MAY HE ADD.` · `RACHEL GAVE LEAH THE SIGNS.` · then, large: `RACHEL WEEPING FOR HER CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Name one thing you honestly long for, not what you're supposed to want: a child, a partner, a healed body, a job, a reconciliation, a home. Say it to yourself plainly, the way Rachel did, without dressing it up or apologizing, and notice where the longing sits in your body. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer just as it is.
Rachel's longing. Years of waiting, rivalry out in the open, a sister protected, and at last Joseph: may He add.
Your line: long honestly. Even Joseph's name, may He add, still longs. Day fifty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Jews read Rachel's story in the Torah portion Vayetze and hear Jeremiah's words about Rachel weeping on Rosh Hashanah; many people, especially women hoping for children, visit Rachel's Tomb near Bethlehem to pray.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 30:1, 30:2 and 30:22.
Naphtali's explanation (30:8) and Joseph's (30:24) are paraphrased.
Rachel giving Leah the signs: Megillah 13b / Bava Batra 123a. Confirm.
Lamentations Rabbah proem 24: patriarchs and Moses plead; God relents for Rachel's sake because she overcame jealousy. Confirm.
Jeremiah 31 verse numbering differs between JPS 1917 (31:14–16) and Christian Bibles (31:15–17). Paraphrased; confirm the ref.
Jeremiah 31 read as the haftarah on the second day of Rosh Hashanah (in howItsDone). Confirm.
Rachel's Tomb near Bethlehem as a place of prayer for fertility: confirm; politically sensitive location, described neutrally.
